lines: Lecture seven: biosensors. Let's build one.
At the bottom is the transducer. On top, a nanomaterial layer holds the receptors, here antibodies.
Around them float the analyte we want to detect, and other molecules that look similar.
The receptor binds its analyte like a lock and key. The look-alike molecules do not fit, and they bounce off. Ignoring them is called selectivity.
The binding changes something. Here, electrons start to flow.
The transducer converts that biological signal into a readable electrical signal.
Learn the parts.
The receptor, also called the biocatalyst, can be an enzyme, an antibody, a nucleic acid, or a cell.
The transducer converts the biological signal into a quantifiable, readable signal, usually electrical.
Now his traps. Is the antigen a receptor? No. The antigen is the analyte.
Is a thermal transducer a receptor? No. It is a transducer.
Biosensors work in vivo, inside the body, like a sensor on a pacemaker, or ex vivo, outside the body, like a glucose meter or a health watch.
Nanomaterials improve two layers of a biosensor.
In the first layer, nanofibers, functionalized nanoparticles and two-dimensional sheets like graphene stabilize the bioreceptors on the transducer.
In the second layer, nano-enabled transistors improve the transducer. Carbon nanotubes and graphene stay conductive at tiny sizes.
So the whole biosensor can shrink. That is what made wearable and implantable sensors possible.
He asked you to memorize three transducers, and said he will most probably ask them.
Amperometric: it measures the current, which is proportional to the bioreaction.
Calorimetric, or thermal: it measures the heat produced or absorbed.
Optical: it measures the change in light intensity when a specific reaction happens.
His own wrong option: an amperometric biosensor measures heat. No. It measures current.
Last, the performance parameters.
Selectivity: detecting the target analyte in the presence of other interfering species.
Sensitivity: how sharply the signal changes when the analyte concentration changes.
Response time: how long the sensor takes to settle at a reliable value.
Limit of detection: the minimum concentration it can detect. Lower is better, because early diagnosis means finding very small amounts.
Accuracy means reproducibility and reliability. Durability means keeping the signal over time.
Two traps. Selectivity is not how sharply the signal changes. That is sensitivity. And the limit of detection is the minimum, never the maximum.
